title: Science and Technology: a Blessing or a Curse?
description: Science and inventions, and the language a scientific page is written in: the three verbs the module opposes — discover something that was already there, invent something that never existed, originate a new idea or method — beside science, technology, applied and pure science, ingenuity, device, nano technology and surgery; the inventions the book dates and the people it credits with them, from the air conditioner to the compact disk, and the vocabulary of medical research, from dialysis and diagnosis to gene therapy, chromosome, germline, designer gene, genetic testing, DNA testing, blood clotting, cloning, ethics, issue and controversial; the negative prefixes, with the one Latin prefix whose spelling follows the first letter of its word — il- before l, im- before m, p and b, ir- before r and in- before the rest — beside un- and dis-, which follow no letter rule at all, mis-, which says the action was done wrongly, and de-, which reverses it; the eight patterns of compound adjective set out in the book's grammar summary, with the number-and-noun and noun-and-participle blocks that scientific writing lives on, the singular noun inside the block and the choice between the -ing form and the past participle; the modals of the module — can and can't, may and might, must and mustn't, should, and needn't for the absence of necessity — each with the bare infinitive after it; the main stress in two-part expressions; the pairs of opposites of the listening section and the nouns built on its verbs, from diagnosis, choice and proof to suspicion and curiosity; reading a science page, with trigger, dismiss, rule out, leap, prick, decapitate, poultry, patch and the two meanings of strain, and the three verdicts true, false and not mentioned; approving, disapproving and doubting out loud, with I'd rather do one thing than another; and writing a text that persuades, judged by its genre, its expected readers and its purpose
